standard.title: Interact in classroom routines and personal introductions
standard.description: interact in classroom-related routines and personal introductions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have used formulaic expressions and communicated personal meaning in supported interactions (AC9LCHF01). They can respond to familiar classroom instructions and share simple personal information with support. They have not yet participated in sustained two-way classroom exchanges, managed requests and responses, or used the target language independently for the full range of classroom social routines.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students interact in classroom-related routines and personal introductions using appropriate greetings, terms of address, requests and formulaic expressions, with growing independence.

nodes.label: Greetings, address and classroom routine language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use appropriate greetings and terms of address for different people and times of day, and respond to classroom routine instructions.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least two contextually appropriate greetings or address forms, and respond correctly to at least three classroom routine instructions.
nodes.typical_width: Use greetings appropriate to time of day and relationship (teacher, peers); respond to routine classroom instructions with appropriate action or language; use formulaic exclamations spontaneously in peer interaction; distinguish between formal address to teachers and informal address to peers.
wider: Compare greeting conventions in the target language with English and another language known in the class — identify what changes across contexts (time of day, relationship, formality)
Identify which languages they know and are learning, discussing how greetings differ across the languages they speak at home and at school
nodes.hinge_reason: Greetings, address forms and routine classroom language are the entry conditions for all classroom participation. Students who cannot manage these conventions cannot engage in the exchanges, introductions or collaborative activities that follow in this and subsequent descriptors.

response_modes.reason: Routine language must become automatic for classroom participation to flow. Repeated daily use of greeting and address conventions — not occasional practice — builds the fluency that allows students to focus attention on content rather than form in later interaction tasks.

success_criteria: Uses an appropriate greeting and address form when initiating or responding to a classroom exchange
Responds correctly to at least three different classroom routine instructions through action or language

nodes.label: Personal information and introductions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can share and request personal information in a structured introduction exchange, using modelled sentence structures.
nodes.minimum_width: Share at least three pieces of personal information (e.g. name, age, school, family) and ask a peer for at least one piece of information using a modelled question form.
nodes.typical_width: Participate in personal introduction exchanges — sharing and requesting information about name, age, class, school, family and interests; use puppets, role-play or paired exchange structures to support the interaction; identify which languages they know and are learning.
wider: Conduct an extended role-play introduction exchange incorporating both personal information sharing and questions, sustaining the exchange for at least four turns
Create a bilingual personal profile combining target language and English, presenting it to the class or a small group

response_modes.reason: Personal introduction exchanges are context-dependent — students need to practise the same information-sharing moves across different partners, formats and purposes (face-to-face, puppet play, digital) to build flexible use rather than memorised performance.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Background learners have rich personal and family stories to share. Width investment in personal introduction tasks activates this authentic communicative resource and builds the confidence to use target language for genuine self-expression, not only rehearsed exchange.
success_criteria: Shares at least three pieces of personal information using target language sentence structures
Asks at least one question to request personal information from a partner

nodes.label: Requests, thanks and everyday social expressions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use polite requests, thanks, apologies and expressions of likes and dislikes in familiar classroom and social contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least two formulaic social expressions appropriately in context — for example, making a polite request, thanking someone, or expressing a like or dislike.
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of social expressions across everyday classroom interactions — polite requests, thanks, apologies, expressions of preference — with appropriate manner and register; begin to use exclamations and formulaic responses spontaneously in peer interaction.
wider: Compare the politeness conventions of the target language with English — identify where the same communicative act (e.g. requesting, thanking) requires different forms or gestures
Role-play a series of short social interactions (e.g. asking to borrow something, thanking a peer, apologising) demonstrating appropriate language and gesture for each

response_modes.reason: Social expression use integrates greeting conventions (node 1) and personal exchange skills (node 2) into the broader repertoire of classroom social language. The teaching investment is in creating authentic occasions for these expressions — not drills, but real moments of requesting, thanking and responding.

success_criteria: Uses at least two different social expressions (request, thanks, apology, or preference) appropriately in a real or role-play context
Demonstrates appropriate manner or gesture alongside the verbal expression
